propositions.text: Applicant challenges Immigration Officer's refusal of permanent residence due to inadmissibility for serious criminality under IRPA s. 36(1)(c)
propositions.quote: The Applicant, selected under the Ontario Provincial Nominee Program (“PNP”), challenges an Immigration Officer’s decision refusing his application for permanent residence on the basis the he is inadmissible to Canada for serious criminality pursuant to s. 36(1)(c) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 [IRPA].

propositions.text: Officer failed to conduct proper analysis under s. 36(1)(c), so Application will be allowed
propositions.quote: I agree that the Officer failed to conduct a proper analysis as required under that provision, and therefore will allow this Application.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant challenges refusal of permanent residence for serious criminality inadmissibility; court finds Officer failed proper analysis and allows Application.

propositions.text: Applicant is Jamaican citizen who applied for permanent residence in Canada via Ontario PNP on January 19, 2016
propositions.quote: The Applicant is a citizen of Jamaica who, on January 19, 2016, applied for permanent residence in Canada through the Ontario PNP.

propositions.text: Applicant revealed he applied for US passport in 2007 using falsified birth certificate and declared truthfulness under penalty of perjury
propositions.quote: The Applicant revealed that, while living in the United States in 2007, he had applied for an American passport using a falsified birth certificate. By signing his passport application, the Applicant declared under penalty of perjury that the information and documents contained therein were truthful and correct.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant is Jamaican who applied for Canadian permanent residence and revealed 2007 US passport application with falsified birth certificate.

propositions.text: Applicant charged with three US federal offences related to passport and perjury, pled to lesser charge of false statement
propositions.quote: He was subsequently charged with three federal offences under Title 18 of the US Penal Code: (i) making false statement in application and use of passport (18 USC § 1542 (1944)), (ii) making a false representation of US citizenship (18 USC § 911 (1996)), and (iii) perjury (18 USC § 1621 (2011)). The Applicant signed a plea deal for the lesser charge of “making a false statement in application and use of passport”; the disposition of the other charges was thus suspended.

propositions.text: Applicant sentenced to time-served and two years probation but chose deportation to Jamaica instead of probation
propositions.quote: He was sentenced to time-served and two years’ probation. Rather than serve his probation, he opted for deportation to Jamaica.

propositions.text: Applicant built successful computer business over next 14 years and was selected by Ontario PNP based on experience
propositions.quote: It was during the next 14 years that the Applicant built a successful computer business and was selected on the basis of his experience by the Ontario PNP.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant charged with US offences, pled to false statement, sentenced, deported, then built business and was selected by Ontario PNP.

propositions.text: Canadian Immigration Officer in Mexico City assessed application and sent procedural fairness letter on June 27, 2019 about potential inadmissibility for perjury charge
propositions.quote: A Canadian Immigration Officer (“Officer”) stationed in Mexico City assessed the permanent residence application. On June 27, 2019, the Officer notified the Applicant via a procedural fairness letter (“PFL”) of his potential inadmissibility to Canada in relation to the charge for perjury.

propositions.text: Officer indicated US perjury offence could correspond to Canadian Criminal Code ss. 131, 139, or 140 and gave Applicant 60 days to respond
propositions.quote: The Officer indicated that the offence, had it been committed in Canada, could be punishable under ss. 131, 139, or 140 of the Criminal Code of Canada, RSC 1985, c C-46 [Criminal Code]. He gave the Applicant 60 days to respond.

propositions.text: Applicant responded to procedural fairness letter on July 12, 2019
propositions.quote: A response was received on July 12, 2019.

paragraphs.summary: Officer in Mexico City sent procedural fairness letter about perjury inadmissibility; Applicant responded July 12, 2019.

propositions.text: Officer found Applicant inadmissible on September 23, 2019, equating US perjury offence to Canadian perjury under s. 131
propositions.quote: On September 23, 2019, the Officer found the Applicant inadmissible to Canada and rejected the application for permanent residence. He determined that the underlying circumstances of the US offence of perjury (“US Perjury”) were consistent with the indictable offence of perjury found under s. 131 of the Criminal Code (“Canadian Perjury”), in that both offences required that the accused has intended to mislead by knowingly making a false statement by affidavit.

paragraphs.summary: Officer found Applicant inadmissible, equating US perjury to Canadian perjury under s. 131.

propositions.text: Officer found Applicant made false affidavit statement with intent to mislead, matching Canadian perjury elements
propositions.quote: The Officer found that the Applicant had made a false statement by affidavit with intent to mislead.

propositions.text: Officer concluded Canadian perjury punishable by 14-year max imprisonment, so Applicant inadmissible under IRPA s. 36(1)(c)
propositions.quote: Had those circumstances arisen in Canada, the Officer determined that they would have given rise to Canadian Perjury, punishable by a 14-year maximum term of imprisonment. He thus concluded that the Applicant was inadmissible under s. 36(1)(c) of IRPA.

propositions.text: Officer did not analyze ss. 139 and 140 of Criminal Code
propositions.quote: The Officer did not perform any analysis in relation to ss. 139 and 140 of the Criminal Code.

paragraphs.summary: Officer found Applicant made false affidavit statement with intent, equated to Canadian perjury punishable by 14 years, and found inadmissible under s. 36(1)(c).

propositions.text: Only Applicant's inadmissibility assessment is at issue, subject to reasonableness review
propositions.quote: Only the assessment of the Applicant’s inadmissibility is at issue in this Application, which attracts a reasonableness review (Garcia v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2021 FC 141 at para 5 [Garcia]; Clarke v Canada (Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness), 2021 FC 128 at para 4 [Clarke]; Randhawa v Canada (Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness), 2020 FC 905 at para 19 [Randhawa]).

paragraphs.summary: Only Applicant's inadmissibility assessment is at issue, reviewed for reasonableness.

propositions.text: Decision must be justified, transparent, intelligible in rationale and outcome per Vavilov
propositions.quote: The decision must be justified, transparent, and intelligible under its facts and the law, in both its rationale and outcome: Vavilov v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2019 SCC 65 at paras 83, 99 [Vavilov].

propositions.text: Statutory interpretation examined in light of whole decision, officer's reasons, and outcome
propositions.quote: In this context, matters of statutory interpretation are not treated uniquely, but are examined in light of the decision as a whole, the officer’s reasons, and the outcome: Clarke at para 4; Vavilov at paras 115-116.

paragraphs.summary: Decision must be justified and intelligible; statutory interpretation examined in context of whole decision and reasons.

propositions.text: IRPA s. 36(1)(c) defines inadmissibility for serious criminality for acts outside Canada that are offences where committed and would be offences in Canada punishable by 10+ years
propositions.quote: Pursuant to IRPA s. 36(1)(c), a foreign national is inadmissible for serious criminality if there are reasonable grounds to believe that they committed an act outside of Canada that is an offence where it was committed and, if committed in Canada, would constitute an offence under an Act of Parliament punishable by a maximum term of imprisonment of 10 years or more.

propositions.text: IRPA ss. 33 and 36(1) set out rules of interpretation and serious criminality inadmissibility provisions
propositions.quote: The two key IRPA provisions are ss. 33 and 36(1) which read as follows: Rules of interpretation Interprétation 33 The facts that constitute inadmissibility under sections 34 to 37 include facts arising from omissions and, unless otherwise provided, include facts for which there are reasonable grounds to believe that they have occurred, are occurring or may occur. ... Serious criminality Grande criminalité 36 (1) A permanent resident or a foreign national is inadmissible on grounds of serious criminality for ...

paragraphs.summary: IRPA s. 36(1)(c) defines serious criminality inadmissibility for acts outside Canada that are offences there and would be offences in Canada punishable by 10+ years.

propositions.text: Reasonable grounds to believe means more than suspicion but less than balance of probabilities, based on compelling credible info
propositions.quote: “Reasonable grounds to believe”, set out in s. 33 represents “more than a mere suspicion”, but less than a balance of probabilities; reasonable grounds exist “where there is an objective basis for the belief which is based on compelling and credible information”: Mugesera v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2005 SCC 40 at paras 111, 114 [Mugesera]; Garcia at para 11.

propositions.text: Standard applies to facts, not law; facts must show offence does, not could, exist under s. 36(1)(c)
propositions.quote: The standard only applies to questions of fact, not questions of law. In other words, when applying the facts to s. 36(1)(c), the facts must show that they do, as opposed to could, constitute an offence (Mugesera at para 116; Garcia at para 11).

paragraphs.summary: Reasonable grounds means more than suspicion but less than balance of probabilities; applies to facts, which must show offence does exist.

propositions.text: First question: whether reasonable grounds existed to believe Applicant committed US offence of perjury by knowingly making false declaration
propositions.quote: The first is a question of fact, namely whether there existed reasonable grounds for the Officer to believe that the Applicant supplied a falsified birth certificate, and knowingly and willingly made a false declaration in his passport application under penalty of perjury.

propositions.text: This would establish reasonable grounds to believe Applicant committed US perjury offence
propositions.quote: This would establish that the Officer had reasonable grounds to believe that the Applicant had committed an act in the US that was an offence in the US (i.e., US Perjury in these circumstances).

paragraphs.summary: First issue is whether reasonable grounds existed to believe Applicant committed US perjury offence by knowingly making false declaration.

propositions.text: Second question: whether facts meet essential elements of Canadian perjury offence chosen by Officer
propositions.quote: The second question, one of application of the facts to the statute, is whether the essential elements of the criminal provision chosen by the Officer – Canadian Perjury – have been made out.

propositions.text: Officer must determine if facts underlying US offence give rise to Canadian perjury under reasonable grounds standard
propositions.quote: As explained above, under this question of law, the Officer must determine whether the facts underlying the US offence, having been demonstrated on the reasonable grounds to believe standard, do indeed give rise to Canadian Perjury.

propositions.text: Thorough examination of Canadian offence elements required (Ghahraman-Ebrahimi v Canada)
propositions.quote: This second question requires a thorough examination of the elements of the Canadian offence (Ghahraman-Ebrahimi v Canada (Attorney General), 2020 FC 746 at para 47).

paragraphs.summary: Second issue is whether facts meet Canadian perjury elements; Officer must thoroughly examine Canadian offence elements under reasonable grounds standard.

propositions.text: Both parties agree s. 36 equivalency analysis compares foreign and Canadian offences as refined in Hill
propositions.quote: Both parties agree that s. 36 admissibility has traditionally engaged an “equivalency analysis” comparing the foreign and the Canadian provision, as refined by the Federal Court of Appeal in Hill v Canada (Minister of Employment & Immigration) (1987), 73 NR 315, 1987 CarswellNat 15 (WL Can) (CA) [Hill cited to WL Can].

propositions.text: Hill provides three methods for equivalency analysis: compare wording, examine evidence, or combine both
propositions.quote: Hill provides for three methods to perform the analysis (at para 16): Comparing of the precise wording in each statute both through documents and, if available, through the evidence of an expert or experts in the foreign law and determining therefrom the essential ingredients of the respective offences; Examining the evidence adduced before the adjudicator, both oral and documentary, to ascertain whether or not that evidence was sufficient to establish that the essential ingredients of the offence in Canada had been proven in the foreign proceedings, whether precisely described in the initiating documents or in the statutory provisions in the same words or not; or Using a combination of one and two.

paragraphs.summary: Parties agree s. 36 equivalency analysis compares foreign and Canadian offences using Hill's three methods.

propositions.text: At minimum, second Hill method applies here: ascertain if essential ingredients of Canadian offence proven
propositions.quote: while there is some debate about the requirement for an equivalency analysis when faced with a s. 36(1)(c) allegation, at a minimum the second Hill examination applies to this case, namely the need to ascertain whether “the essential ingredients of the offence in Canada have been proven”.

paragraphs.summary: At minimum, second Hill method applies: ascertain if essential ingredients of Canadian offence proven.

propositions.text: Brannson stresses importance of comparing essential elements of foreign and Canadian offences
propositions.quote: Brannson v Canada ... stressed the centrality of considering the offence’s essential ingredients ... one must determine the essential elements of each and be satisfied that these essential elements correspond.

propositions.text: Differences in wording expected but essential elements must correspond; example given about letters or circulars
propositions.quote: One must, of course, expect differences in the wording of statutory offences in different countries. I cannot, however, even with this in mind, escape the conclusion that the sending or transmission of "letters or circulars" is an essential element of the Canadian offence.

paragraphs.summary: Brannson emphasizes comparing essential elements of offences; wording differences expected but essential elements must correspond.

propositions.text: Li explains equivalency analysis requires comparing factual and legal criteria and definitions including defences
propositions.quote: Li explained that it requires a comparison of the “factual and legal criteria for establishing the offence both abroad and in Canada”. The Court of Appeal further explained that a “comparison of the “essential elements” of the respective offences requires a comparison of the definitions of those offences including defences particular to those offences or those classes of offences”.

paragraphs.summary: Li explains equivalency analysis requires comparing factual and legal criteria and definitions including defences.

propositions.text: Applicant deemed inadmissible under s. 36(1)(c), which differs from s. 36(1)(b) by applying to acts committed, not convictions
propositions.quote: Applicant was deemed inadmissible under s. 36(1)(c), s. 36(1)(c) employs very similar language to s. 36(1)(b). The difference is that s. 36(1)(b) deems inadmissible a foreign national who has been “convicted” of a foreign offence, while s. 36(1)(c) applies to those who have merely “committed” a foreign offence.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant inadmissible under s. 36(1)(c), which applies to acts committed, unlike s. 36(1)(b) for convictions.

propositions.text: Officer's procedural fairness letter mentioned conviction or commission, but GCMS notes show inadmissibility under s. 36(1)(c) for commission only
propositions.quote: In the PFL, the Officer originally informed the Applicant of his potential inadmissibility to Canada under IRPA s. 36(1) for having committed or having been convicted of an offence. However, the Officer’s notes logged in the Global Case Management System (“GCMS Notes”) make clear that the Applicant was deemed inadmissible under s. 36(1)(c) – for having committed a foreign offence, and not for a US conviction under s. 36(1)(b).

paragraphs.summary: Officer's letter mentioned conviction or commission, but notes show inadmissibility under s. 36(1)(c) for commission only.

propositions.text: Some judges disagree that full equivalency analysis is required under s. 36(1)(c)
propositions.quote: I note, however, that certain judges of this Court have disagreed that a full equivalency analysis needs be done under s. 36(1)(c): Garcia at paras 49-50; Nguesso v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 FC 879 at paras 208-210; Victor v Canada (Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness), 2013 FC 979 at paras 35-37.

propositions.text: Garcia holds s. 36(1)(c) requires act be offence where committed and offence punishable by 10+ years in Canada, no equivalency needed
propositions.quote: As Justice Nicholas McHaffie held in Garcia, at para 50: The analysis under paragraph 36(1)(c) of the IRPA, however, pertains not to a conviction outside Canada or even a charge, but to an act committed by the individual. The paragraph has two requirements. First, the act must be “an offence” where it was committed. Second, the act must constitute an offence punishable by a maximum term of imprisonment of at least 10 years, if it were committed in Canada. Unlike paragraph 36(1)(b), the paragraph does not on its face require that there be any equivalence between the offences in the two jurisdictions; simply that the act be “an offence” where it was committed, and constitute “an offence” with a particular punishment in Canada.

paragraphs.summary: Some judges disagree full equivalency analysis needed under s. 36(1)(c); Garcia holds only act must be offence where committed and punishable in Canada.

propositions.text: Other decisions hold equivalency analysis is required under s. 36(1)(c) to establish inadmissibility
propositions.quote: Garcia points out that other decisions have held that an equivalency analysis is required to establish inadmissibility under s. 36(1)(c). These cases include Randhawa at para 31; Cruz v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2020 FC 455 at paras 42-43; Singh v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2019 FC 946 at paras 16-17; and Pardhan v Canada (Minister of Citizenship & Immigration), 2007 FC 756 at paras 9-10.

paragraphs.summary: Other decisions hold equivalency analysis is required under s. 36(1)(c) to establish inadmissibility.

propositions.text: Court directed parties' attention to Garcia issue and allowed post-hearing submissions, which are considered in these Reasons.
propositions.quote: During the hearing, this Court directed the Parties’ attention to this issue. Given that the parties had not commented on Garcia, both were provided with the opportunity to make post-hearing submissions, and both parties did so. These Reasons take those post-hearing submissions into account.

paragraphs.summary: The Court directed parties to address Garcia and considered their post-hearing submissions in these Reasons.

propositions.text: Applicant submits equivalency analysis under s. 36(1)(c) is not dispositive but officer must consider essential elements of Canadian offence, which officer failed to do here.
propositions.quote: the Applicant submits that the jurisprudence clearly demonstrates it is unreasonable for an officer to fail to turn their mind to the essential elements of the Canadian Offence. In this case, the Applicant argues that the Officer failed to do.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues officer unreasonably failed to consider essential elements of Canadian offence under s. 36(1)(c).

propositions.text: Respondent agrees Garcia is not dispositive and that s. 36(1)(c) requires analysis of whether foreign offence facts satisfy Canadian offence essential elements.
propositions.quote: They also agree that s. 36(1)(c) requires an officer to analyze whether the underlying facts of the foreign offence satisfy the essential elements of the Canadian offence.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent agrees s. 36(1)(c) requires analysis of foreign offence facts against Canadian offence elements and Garcia is not dispositive.

propositions.text: Court agrees Garcia divergence need not be decided; Officer's analysis was fundamentally flawed and unreasonable under either approach.
propositions.quote: I agree with the parties that the Court need not pronounce on the divergence raised in Garcia, as it is not dispositive in this case. In my view, the Officer’s analysis was fundamentally flawed such that it cannot be considered reasonable under either approach.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Officer's analysis fundamentally flawed and unreasonable, so Garcia divergence need not be decided.

propositions.text: Traditional equivalency analysis under s. 36(1)(c) requires identifying and comparing essential elements of foreign and Canadian offences, then establishing if foreign offence facts give rise to Canadian offence.
propositions.quote: The traditional view favouring the equivalency analysis under s. 36(1)(c) requires the officer to complete two tasks: (i) identify and compare the constituent or essential elements of both the foreign and the Canadian offence; and (ii) establish whether the underlying circumstances of the foreign offence do in fact give rise to the Canadian offence.

paragraphs.summary: Traditional equivalency analysis requires comparing essential elements and establishing if foreign offence facts give rise to Canadian offence.

propositions.text: Garcia view does not require offence comparison but requires examining if foreign offence facts give rise to Canadian offence.
propositions.quote: The view favoured in Garcia does not require a comparison of the offences in play, because the equivalency of the offences is not conclusive. However, this view imposes a requirement that the adjudicator adequately examine whether the underlying circumstances of the foreign offence do in fact give rise to the Canadian offence.

paragraphs.summary: Garcia approach requires examining if foreign offence facts give rise to Canadian offence without comparing offences.

propositions.text: Minimum requirement is that officer adequately justify how foreign offence facts give rise to Canadian offence.
propositions.quote: Therefore, the lowest common denominator between those two approaches is to require – at a minimum – that an officer adequately demonstrate or justify how the underlying circumstances of the foreign offence give rise to the Canadian offence.

propositions.text: Officer must engage with essential elements of Canadian offence selected for inadmissibility determination.
propositions.quote: the officer must nevertheless engage with the essential elements of the Canadian offence that has been selected for the purposes of determining inadmissibility.

propositions.text: Officer commits reviewable error if failing to explain how Canadian offence elements are met or if conclusion is not reasonably justified by facts and law.
propositions.quote: the officer will commit a reviewable error if they fail to properly explain how the elements of the Canadian offence were met, or where their conclusion in relation to the Canadian offence is not reasonably justified in light of the facts and the law.

paragraphs.summary: Officer must justify how foreign offence facts give rise to Canadian offence and engage with essential elements; failure is reviewable error.

propositions.text: Applicant argues Officer's s. 36(1)(c) analysis was grossly deficient, only comparing offence titles and noting system similarity without addressing essential Canadian offence elements.
propositions.quote: the Officer’s s. 36(1)(c) analysis was grossly deficient, merely comparing the titles of the offences, noting a similarity between the US and Canadian legal systems and, from there, deciding that the two offences were equivalent. There was no engagement in addressing the essential elements of the Canadian offence.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant contends Officer's analysis was deficient, only superficially comparing offence titles without addressing essential Canadian offence elements.

propositions.text: Applicant submits Canadian Perjury is narrower than US Perjury, applying only to false statements in court or judicial proceedings, so essential ingredients differ.
propositions.quote: Canadian Perjury applies only to false statements made in court or in relation to a judicial proceeding, and thus cannot apply to false declarations made in relation to a passport application. Thus, the essential ingredients of the two offences are different.

propositions.text: Applicant argues Criminal Code ss. 139 and 140 are inapplicable as they require judicial proceeding or peace officer investigation, absent here.
propositions.quote: The other two Criminal Code offences cited by the Officer – s. 139 (“obstructing justice”) and s. 140 (“public mischief”) – are not applicable to these circumstances because they did not involve a judicial proceeding or the investigation of a peace officer.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues Canadian Perjury is narrower than US Perjury and other cited offences are inapplicable due to lack of judicial proceeding.

propositions.text: Applicant says Officer should have selected s. 57(2) false statement in relation to passport as Canadian offence, analyzed under s. 36(2) ordinary criminality, leading to deemed rehabilitation and no inadmissibility.
propositions.quote: Instead, the Applicant indicates that the Officer should have selected “false statement in relation to passport” (s. 57(2) of the Criminal Code) as the Canadian offence, which is punishable on summary conviction for a term not exceeding two years’ imprisonment. Had that been the case, the analysis of which would have been conducted under IRPA s. 36(2) (which I will refer to as “ordinary criminality”) and not s. 36(1), the Applicant would not be inadmissible by virtue of deemed rehabilitation under IRPA s. 36(3)(c), and ss. 18(1)-(2). Together, these provisions deem that rehabilitation occurs 10 years after conviction for s. 36(2) ordinary criminality.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues Officer should have selected s. 57(2) offence, analyzed under s. 36(2), leading to deemed rehabilitation and no inadmissibility.

propositions.text: Respondent submits Officer's analysis was reasonable; Canadian Perjury is not restricted to false declarations in court or judicial proceedings, so essential ingredients are the same.
propositions.quote: Principally, the Minister argues that Canadian Perjury is not restricted in application to false declarations made in court or in relation to court proceedings. Accordingly, the essential ingredients of the two offences are the same, and the Officer’s conclusion on inadmissibility was reasonable.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues Canadian Perjury is not limited to court declarations and Officer's conclusion was reasonable.

propositions.text: Respondent acknowledges s. 57(2) might be better comparator but IRPA does not require selecting offence with most favourable immigration consequences or closest match.
propositions.quote: IRPA does not require that an officer compare the foreign offence with a Canadian offence that would result in the most favourable immigration consequences for an applicant, nor with an offence that most exactly matches or is most similar to the foreign offence.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent acknowledges s. 57(2) might be better comparator but IRPA does not require best or closest offence match.

propositions.text: Court finds Officer's analysis fell below minimum standard common to both approaches in Garcia in two ways: no engagement with essential elements and erroneous conclusion Canadian Perjury made out.
propositions.quote: the Officer’s analysis fell well below the minimum standard common to both approaches highlighted in Garcia in two ways. First, while the Officer recited s. 131 of the Criminal Code, he failed to engage with its essential elements, and thus to explain how the underlying facts would give rise to the offence. Second, the Officer’s conclusion that the underlying facts give rise to Canadian Perjury is erroneous.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Officer's analysis deficient for failing to engage essential elements and erroneously concluding Canadian Perjury made out.

propositions.text: Canadian Perjury provision s. 131(1) requires false statement under oath or solemn affirmation before authorized person, knowledge statement is false, and intent to mislead.
propositions.quote: Perjury Parjure 131 (1) Subject to subsection (3), every one commits perjury who, with intent to mislead, makes before a person who is authorized by law to permit it to be made before him a false statement under oath or solemn affirmation, by affidavit, solemn declaration or deposition or orally, knowing that the statement is false.

propositions.text: s. 131(2) states offence applies whether or not statement is made in judicial proceeding.
propositions.quote: (2) Subsection (1) applies, whether or not a statement referred to in that subsection is made in a judicial proceeding.

paragraphs.summary: Court states Canadian Perjury requires false statement under oath before authorized person, knowledge of falsity, intent to mislead; applies inside or outside judicial proceedings.

propositions.text: Canadian Perjury has three elements: false statement under oath before authorized person, knowledge statement is false, and intent to mislead; it is a mens rea offence.
propositions.quote: The text of the provision reveals three constituent elements for Canadian Perjury: (i) a false statement made under oath or solemn affirmation before a person authorized by law to permit it to be made before them; (ii) knowledge that the statement is false at the time it is made; and (iii) an intent to mislead (see Calder v The Queen, [1960] SCR 892 at 897; R v Wilson, 2011 ONSC 3385 at para 36). Thus, Canadian Perjury is a mens rea offence requiring the Crown to establish the accused’s intent to mislead.

propositions.text: Canadian Perjury can occur outside judicial proceedings: Criminal Code s. 131(2); R c Vanier, 2018 ONSC 2714 at para 11.
propositions.quote: The offence can occur outside the context of a judicial proceeding: Criminal Code, at s 131(2); R c Vanier, 2018 ONSC 2714 at para 11.

paragraphs.summary: Canadian Perjury requires false statement under oath, knowledge of falsity, intent to mislead; can occur outside judicial proceedings.

propositions.text: Officer's GCMS Notes discuss US Perjury facts and Applicant background but lack discussion on how facts constitute Canadian Perjury; Officer notes system similarity and concludes Canadian Perjury made out.
propositions.quote: The Officer dedicates a considerable portion of the GCMS Notes to the circumstances underlying the US Perjury charge, as well as to the Applicant’s background. However, this commentary on the US is followed by the marked contrast of a dearth of discussion about how those facts would constitute Canadian Perjury. The Officer notes that the “US court system is similar to that of Canada”, and proceeds to conclude that Canadian Perjury has been made out: Section 131 [of the Criminal Code] appears consistent with documents on file. [Applicant], with intent to mislead, made a false statement by affidavit knowing that the statement is false, when applying for a US passport. Max penalty of 14 years. I have also taken account [Criminal Code] 368 and IRPA 122. While I note that [Applicant] may also be inadmissible on these grounds and that an equivalency may be made, based on the information before me and that which was communicated to [Applicant], I have reasonable grounds to believe that [Applicant] is presently inadmissible to Canada under A36(1)(c) for committing an act, mainly perjury, that is an offence where it was committed (the US) and which would constitute an offence under an Act of Parliament (Criminal Code 131) punishable by a maximum term of imprisonment of at least 10 years.

paragraphs.summary: Officer's notes discuss US Perjury facts but lack analysis on Canadian Perjury elements, yet conclude Canadian Perjury made out.

propositions.text: IAD decision holds officer need not select Canadian offence with best immigration consequences, but officer must demonstrate applicability and how offence is made out on facts.
propositions.quote: While that may be, it is nevertheless incumbent on the Officer to (i) demonstrate why the selected Canadian offence is applicable, and (ii) how it is made out on the underlying facts.

propositions.text: IAD decision cited: Canada (Minister of Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness) and Adekunle, Re, 2017 CarswellNat 4435 (WL Can) (Imm App Div).
propositions.quote: The Respondent relies on a decision from the Immigration Appeal Division (“IAD”) of the Immigration and Refugee Board for the proposition that an Immigration Officer need not select, for the purposes of inadmissibility, the Canadian offence which would lead to the best immigration consequences for the Applicant (Canada (Minister of Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness) and Adekunle, Re, 2017 CarswellNat 4435 (WL Can) (Imm App Div), citing, Canada (Minister of Citizenship & Immigration) v Canada (Immigration & Refugee Board - Appeal Division) (1999), 178 FTR 110, 1999 CarswellNat 2486 (WL Can) (TD)).

propositions.text: Officer skipped crucial step of demonstrating applicability and how Canadian offence is made out; wrongly concluded Canadian Perjury made out.
propositions.quote: Here, the Officer skipped this crucial step. Furthermore, in my view, the Officer wrongly concluded that Canadian Perjury was made out.

paragraphs.summary: IAD decision says officer need not pick best offence but must demonstrate applicability and facts; Officer failed and wrongly concluded Canadian Perjury made out.

propositions.text: Court agrees Canadian Perjury can occur outside court process but requires false declaration under oath before authorized person; record lacks indication Applicant was under oath or before authorized person.
propositions.quote: I agree with the Respondent that Canadian Perjury can occur outside of the court process: s. 131(2) of the Criminal Code makes this explicitly clear. However, Canadian Perjury requires that the false declaration was made under oath, before a person authorized by law to receive such oath. The Officer’s GCMS Notes indicate that the Applicant made false statements “by affidavit”, yet nothing on the record indicates that the Applicant was under oath or affirmation at the time he signed the declaration. Nor does the record reveal that the Applicant made the declaration “before a person who is authorized by law to permit it to be made before him”.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Canadian Perjury requires oath before authorized person; record lacks evidence Applicant was under oath or before authorized person.

propositions.text: US Perjury distinguishes false statements under oath and those under penalty of perjury; Canadian Perjury language is not broad enough to cover false declarations like Applicant's.
propositions.quote: For contrast, US Perjury explicitly distinguishes between false statements made under oath to an authorized representative and those made under “penalty of perjury”, the second category being most comparable to the Applicant’s situation. The language of Canadian Perjury, in my view, is not broad enough to capture these circumstances (see, for example, United States of America v Quintin, [2000] OTC 170, [2000] OJ No 791 at para 109 (Sup Ct J), in which the Ontario Superior Court of Justice held that Canadian Perjury did not apply to false statements in a tax return).

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Canadian Perjury language too narrow to cover false declarations under penalty of perjury like Applicant's, unlike US Perjury.

propositions.text: Respondent argues lying in passport application can meet Canadian Perjury definition, citing United States of America v Sosa, 2011 ABQB 534.
propositions.quote: The Respondent argues that lying in a passport application can meet the definition of Canadian Perjury, and, in support of the proposition, cites United States of America v Sosa, 2011 ABQB 534 at paras 11, 26-27, 34 [Sosa], leave to appeal to the ABCA ref’d, 2012 ABCA 242, leave to appeal to the SCC ref’d, [2012] SCCA No 433.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues lying in passport application can constitute Canadian Perjury, citing Sosa case.

propositions.text: Sosa reinforces my conclusions above regarding Canadian Perjury equivalency.
propositions.quote: Sosa reinforces my conclusions above.

propositions.text: Sosa involved a Guatemalan national charged with making false declarations under oath for US naturalization, equivalent to Canadian Perjury.
propositions.quote: the Court determined that a Guatemalan national, sought for extradition and prosecution by the United States Government for making false declarations while attempting to become a naturalized American citizen, had committed an offence equivalent to Canadian Perjury.

propositions.text: The individual knowingly made false statements in application documents and interviews under penalty of perjury.
propositions.quote: The individual knowingly made false statements in his application documents and during various interviews with immigration officials under penalty of perjury.

propositions.text: During an interview, the individual swore under oath that his application information was true and correct.
propositions.quote: during an interview with a naturalization examiner, the individual swore under oath that the information contained in his application and shared during his interviews remained true and correct.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Sosa reinforces its conclusions, describing a Guatemalan who made false sworn statements equivalent to Canadian Perjury.

propositions.text: Sosa is distinguishable because the individual made false statements under oath before an authorized person, unlike Mr. Griffiths.
propositions.quote: Sosa is thus distinguishable on the key fact that the individual in question (i) had made false statements, and had done so (ii) while under oath, (iii) before a person authorized by law to receive sworn statements.

propositions.text: The Respondent argues equivalency based on Sosa, but this argument cannot succeed here.
propositions.quote: Thus, the Respondent’s argument on this point cannot succeed.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Sosa differs because the false statements were under oath, so the Respondent's equivalency argument fails.

propositions.text: I am not satisfied the Applicant would have committed Canadian Perjury if his US charge arose in Canada.
propositions.quote: I am not satisfied the Applicant would have committed Canadian Perjury had the underlying circumstances of his US charge arisen in Canada.

propositions.text: The Officer’s conclusion was unreasonable and failed to properly apply facts to Canadian law.
propositions.quote: The Officer’s conclusion was thus unreasonable in light of the facts on the record, and his failure to apply them to the Canadian provision properly.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the Applicant would not have committed Canadian Perjury and finds the Officer's conclusion unreasonable.

propositions.text: The Officer’s decision is unreasonable due to two fatal flaws regarding Canadian Perjury equivalency and essential elements.
propositions.quote: The Officer’s decision is unreasonable regardless of whether an equivalency analysis is required under s. 36(1)(c) by reason of two fatal flaws.

propositions.text: The Officer erroneously concluded the Applicant’s acts would have constituted Canadian Perjury if committed in Canada.
propositions.quote: The Officer erroneously concluded that the underlying circumstances of the acts committed by the Applicant would have given rise to Canadian Perjury, had they arisen in Canada.

propositions.text: The Officer failed to engage with the essential elements of Canadian Perjury and the minimum standard under s. 36(1)(c).
propositions.quote: Combined with his failure to engage with the essential elements of Canadian Perjury, the Officer failed to satisfy the “minimum standard” required under s. 36(1)(c).

propositions.text: The decision lacks justification, transparency, and intelligibility, and is thus unreasonable.
propositions.quote: It follows that the decision does not meet the hallmarks of justification, transparency, and intelligibility, and is thus unreasonable.

propositions.text: The judicial review application is allowed and the matter is remitted for redetermination by another Officer.
propositions.quote: For these reasons, this Application for judicial review is allowed.

propositions.text: This application for judicial review is granted and remitted for redetermination by another Officer.
propositions.quote: This application for judicial review is granted. The matter will be remitted for redetermination by another Officer.

propositions.text: No question of general importance arises for certification.
propositions.quote: The parties proposed no question of general importance for certification, and I agree that none arises.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer's decision unreasonable for two fatal flaws, grants judicial review, and remits the matter for redetermination.
